description:
We are building a web app for farmers in Kyrgyzstan: an interactive map, 40 years of NASA climate data charts, and a comparison of 3 crop rotation options (water / soil / income), plus a "What if +2°C?" mode.

In-person at Ala-Too University. We speak Russian and English.
summary: Jer Salamat ("Healthy Land" in Kyrgyz) is a mobile-first web app in English and Russian that helps farmers in Kyrgyzstan's Chuy Valley (Sokuluk District) adapt their crop rotations using 40 years (1986-2025) of NASA POWER agroclimatology data. A farmer places a pin on their field and answers 5 short questions about current crops, soil, irrigation, summer water shortages and their priority. The app then shows how local air temperature (T2M), precipitation (PRECTOTCORR) and root-zone soil wetness (GWETROOT) have changed since 1986: in Sokuluk the trend is +1.3 °C over 40 years, and 2025 was both the hottest and the driest year on record. It compares the farmer's current rotation with three 4-year alternatives (Water saving, Soil health, Income-focused) on water need and soil health, and explains which NASA indicators and which farmer answers shaped the advice. Every number is labeled by source, a +2 °C scenario is clearly marked as hypothetical, and the app never invents yields, prices or profits.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Jer Salamat turns 40 years of NASA POWER agroclimatology data into a short, field-ready crop rotation guide for farmers in the Chuy Valley (Sokuluk District), Kyrgyzstan. Most of Kyrgyzstan is mountainous, so the flat irrigated farmland of the northern Chuy Valley is scarce and valuable. NASA POWER records for Sokuluk (42.86 N, 74.30 E) show yearly mean air temperature rising by +1.3 °C along the 1986-2025 trend line (+0.32 °C per decade, statistically significant; +1.06 °C comparing 1986-1995 with 2016-2025). Annual precipitation swings between 197 and 599 mm (mean 347 mm/year), and 2025 was both the hottest (15.69 °C) and the driest (197 mm) year in the record. Warmer summers pull more water out of soil and crops, while repeating wheat or water-hungry crops wears the soil out.
HOW IT WORKS
1. Pick a field: search a village, tap a demo location or drop a pin on the map.
2. Answer 5 plain questions: current crops, soil type, irrigation source, how often water runs short in summer, and the farmer's priority (save water, keep soil healthy, grow crops to sell). "I don't know" is always allowed and lowers the confidence rating.
3. See 40 years of NASA climate: the app requests T2M, PRECTOTCORR and GWETROOT from the NASA POWER monthly point API (community AG, 1986-2025), computes yearly series and linear trends with significance tests, and explains them in plain language. An optional +2 °C line is labeled "Hypothetical, not a forecast".
4. Compare rotations: a TypeScript rules engine compares the farmer's current rotation with three 4-year alternatives: Water saving (wheat, beans or peas, barley, wheat), Soil health (alfalfa, alfalfa, wheat, beans or peas) and Income-focused (sugar beet, wheat, potato, beans or peas). Water need uses FAO crop water ranges checked against NASA precipitation; soil impact uses FAO rotation guidance. A "What makes your plan yours" card shows which answers changed the result.
BENEFITS AND IMPACT
Farmers get a clear, honest starting point for a conversation with an agronomist, on a phone, in English or Russian, free and without registration. Every statement is tagged by source (Historical NASA data, Your answers, General guidance, Hypothetical). Verified local yield, price and cost data are not available, so income is shown as "cannot be reliably estimated" instead of invented numbers.
WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
It starts from the farmer, not the dataset: a landing that flies from the globe down to the Chuy Valley, a map pin instead of coordinates, five plain questions, and results written as what to do this season, next season and in 2-3 years.
FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
NASA POWER is a regional grid (about 50 km), so neighbouring farms share the same climate and the farmer's answers personalise the plan. The app never claims that NASA recommends crops; all advice is marked as preliminary guidance to check with a local agronomist.
TOOLS
React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles, Chart.js, Three.js with React Three Fiber, Motion, deployed on Vercel. Source code: https://github.com/Aymanchk/jer-salamat
dataRefs: NASA POWER Monthly Point API (T2M, PRECTOTCORR, GWETROOT; community AG; 1986-2025; Sokuluk 42.86N 74.30E)

FAO Conservation Agriculture: Species Diversification (rotation guidance)
FAO: Soil biology and biological nitrogen fixation
